chapterNote: The psalm of the thirsty soul, and Scripture's classic anatomy of spiritual depression. A son of Korah, exiled somewhere in the northern headwaters country of the Jordan, far from the temple where he once led festival processions, hears the snow-melt torrents of Hermon crashing gorge to gorge and recognizes his own drowning: deep calls to deep, all Your waves and breakers have gone over me. His soul pants like a deer in drought, tears have become his daily bread, and the mockers' question — Where is your God? — works in his bones like a sword. But the psalm's genius is what he does with the despair: he refuses to let his soul do the talking, and talks to his soul instead. Twice the refrain rises — Why are you cast down, O my soul? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him — self-preaching that names the darkness honestly and then overrules it with memory and promise. Even in the flood, the LORD commands His covenant love by day and gives His song in the night; the psalm ends still in the storm, but with the soul under orders.

1.text: For the choir director. A maskil of the sons of Korah. As the deer pants for the flowing streams, so my soul pants for You, O God.
1.amp: To the chief Musician [natsach], Maschil ['a psalm giving instruction', the KJV margin], for the sons [ben] of Korah [Qorach]. As the hart [ayyal — the stag] pants ['brayeth', arag, the KJV margin] after the water [mayim] brooks [aphiq — the stream-channels], so pants [arag] my soul [nephesh] after You, O God [Elohim].
1.notes: arag (H6165) is the audible longing of a parched animal — the KJV margin says 'brayeth': need past the point of silence. The aphiq (H650) is the stream-BED, the channel that ought to hold water; in drought the deer stands where water should be. The nephesh knows that geography.

2.text: My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?
2.amp: My soul [nephesh] thirsts [tsame] for God [Elohim], for the living [chay] God [El]: when shall I come [bo] and appear [raah] before [panim] God?
2.notes: tsame (H6770): thirst, the need that cannot be postponed or substituted. 'The chay El' (H2416, H410), the LIVING God — not the idea of Him, which quenches nothing. 'Appear before God' is festival language for the pilgrim feasts (cf. Exodus 23:17); the exile is asking when he can go to church again, and it reads like a man asking for water.

3.text: My tears have been my bread day and night, while all day long they say to me, 'Where is your God?'
3.amp: My tears [dimah] have been my meat [lechem — my bread] day [yomam] and night [layil], while they continually say [amar] unto me, 'Where is your God [Elohim]?'
3.notes: Tears as lechem (H3899): grief served at every meal, the diet of depression. The taunt 'Where is your Elohim?' is the sword that will return in verse 10 — unanswerable by argument, answerable only by the God who shows up.

4.text: These things I remember as I pour out my soul within me: how I used to walk with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God, with the voice of ringing joy and thanksgiving, a multitude keeping the feast.
4.amp: When I remember [zakar] these things, I pour out [shaphak] my soul [nephesh] in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house [bayith] of God [Elohim], with the voice [qol] of joy [rinnah — ringing cry] and praise [todah — thanksgiving], with a multitude that kept holyday [chagag — danced the festival].
4.notes: zakar (H2142) here wounds: the memory is of leading worship, not merely attending it — the Korahites were the temple's gatekeepers and singers (cf. 1 Chronicles 9:19). shaphak (H8210), poured out like water, the very element his soul is dying for; rinnah and todah (H7440, H8426) and the festival dance (chagag, H2287) all past tense.

5.text: Why are you bowed down, O my soul? Why do you roar and churn within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him for the salvation of His face.
5.amp: Why are you cast down ['bowed', shachah, the KJV margin], O my soul [nephesh]? and why are you disquieted [hamah — roaring, churning like the sea] in me? hope [yachal — wait expectantly] in God [Elohim]: for I shall yet praise [yadah — give thanks to] Him for the help [yeshuah — salvation] of His countenance ['His presence is salvation', panim, the KJV margin].
5.notes: The refrain that made this psalm the church's manual against despair: the man stops listening to himself and starts talking to himself. hamah (H1993) is the sea's roar — the inner weather named without shame — and then the soul is given orders: yachal (H3176), hope. The ground is the panim: His face itself is the yeshuah.

6.text: O my God, my soul is bowed down within me; therefore I will remember You from the land of Jordan, from the peaks of Hermon, from the hill Mizar.
6.amp: O my God [Elohim], my soul [nephesh] is cast down [shachah] within me: therefore will I remember [zakar] You from the land [eretz] of Jordan [Yarden], and of the Hermonites [Chermon], from the hill [har] Mizar ['the little hill', the KJV margin].
6.notes: The sermon of verse 5 does not end the battle — the despair returns in the next breath, and the psalmist deploys his weapon: zakar (H2142), deliberate remembering, from named coordinates. The Yarden headwaters under Hermon are the far north, the opposite corner of the land from Zion: he cannot reach the sanctuary, so he sends memory there instead.

7.text: Deep calls to deep at the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your waves and Your breakers have swept over me.
7.amp: Deep [tehom] calls [qara] unto deep [tehom] at the noise [qol] of Your waterspouts [tsinnor — waterfalls, channels]: all Your waves [mishbar — breakers] and Your billows [gal] are gone [abar] over me.
7.notes: tehom (H8415) is the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2: abyss hailing abyss, the Hermon cataracts in spring flood as a picture of griefs summoning griefs. The possessives are the verse's theology — YOUR waves, YOUR breakers: even the drowning is not outside His ownership. Jonah prayed this verse from inside the fish (cf. Jonah 2:3).

8.text: Yet the LORD will command His covenant kindness in the daytime, and in the night His song will be with me, a prayer to the God of my life.
8.amp: Yet the LORD [YHWH] will command [tsavah] His lovingkindness [chesed — covenant kindness, steadfast love] in the daytime [yomam], and in the night [layil] His song [shir] shall be with me, and my prayer [tephillah] unto the God [El] of my life [chay].
8.notes: The one appearance of the covenant name YHWH (H3068) in the psalm, at its exact center of hope. tsavah (H6680): chesed (H2617) arrives under orders, deployed like a soldier. And the night that once served only tears (v. 3) now carries His shir (H7892) — songs given in the dark are still songs (cf. Job 35:10).

9.text: I will say to God my rock, 'Why have You forgotten me? Why must I walk in mourning under the enemy's oppression?'
9.amp: I will say [amar] unto God [El] my rock [sela — my crag, my cliff], 'Why have You forgotten [shakach] me? why go I mourning [qadar — walking darkened, in mourner's black] because of the oppression [lachats] of the enemy [oyeb]?'
9.notes: Faith's honest grammar: 'my sela' (H5553) and 'why have You shakach (H7911), forgotten me' in one sentence — addressed complaint, not abandoned faith. qadar (H6937) is to go about darkened, the mourner's gait; the psalm permits the question as long as it is asked toward the Rock.

10.text: As with a shattering in my bones, my adversaries reproach me, while all day long they say to me, 'Where is your God?'
10.amp: As with a sword ['killing', retsach, the KJV margin] in my bones [etsem], my enemies [tsarar] reproach [charaph] me; while they say [amar] daily [yom] unto me, 'Where is your God [Elohim]?'
10.notes: The taunt of verse 3 returns at bone depth: retsach (H7524), a murder-blow felt in the etsem (H6106). charaph (H2778) is the reproach-word of Goliath's defiance — the mocking question is warfare, and the psalmist feels every repetition as a fresh thrust.

11.text: Why are you bowed down, O my soul? Why do you roar and churn within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.
11.amp: Why are you cast down [shachah], O my soul [nephesh]? and why are you disquieted [hamah] within me? hope [yachal] in God [Elohim]: for I shall yet praise [yadah] Him, who is the health [yeshuah — the salvation] of my countenance [panim], and my God.
11.notes: The refrain a second time, with one small, enormous change: verse 5 hoped for the salvation of HIS face; verse 11 calls Him the salvation of MY face — His panim lifting mine. The storm has not stopped, but the soul is under orders it now half-believes, and 'my Elohim' is the last word. The refrain sounds once more in Psalm 43:5, this psalm's continuation.
